Eileen Feng Gu (born September 3, 2003, in San Francisco), also known by her Chinese name Gu Ailing (谷爱凌), is an American-born freestyle skier who competes internationally for China and the most decorated female freestyle skier in Olympic history with six medals.[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2) Raised in San Francisco by a Chinese immigrant mother and an American father, Gu began skiing at age three and initially competed for the United States in junior events.[[2]](#ref-2) In October 2019, she announced her intention to represent China starting from the 2020–21 season, citing opportunities to advance women's skiing in that country, though the decision aligned with China's substantial investments in winter sports infrastructure ahead of the Beijing Olympics.[[3]](#ref-3)
Gu rose to global prominence at the [2022 Winter Olympics](/page/2022_Winter_Olympics) in [Beijing](/page/Beijing), where, at age 18, she became the youngest Olympic champion in [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) history by securing gold medals in [big air](/page/Big_air) and [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), along with a silver in [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle)—the first [athlete](/page/Athlete) to medal in all three events at a single Games.[[2]](#ref-2) Her Olympic success followed early wins, including a 2019 FIS [Freestyle Skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) World Cup [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) victory at age 15 and multiple [X Games](/page/X_Games) medals.[[4]](#ref-4) Post-Olympics, she has continued dominating, achieving 20 World Cup wins by February 2026—including a halfpipe victory at Secret Garden in December 2025 (her 19th) and a slopestyle win at Laax in January 2026 (her 20th)—along with a gold medal in women's freeski halfpipe and silver medals in big air and slopestyle at the 2026 Winter Olympics, while maintaining a high podium rate in international competitions.[[1]](#ref-1)[[5]](#ref-5)[[6]](#ref-6)[[7]](#ref-7)
The switch in national allegiance generated significant controversy, particularly in the United States, where detractors viewed it as disloyalty amid geopolitical frictions and China's policies on issues like [Xinjiang](/page/Xinjiang) and [Hong Kong](/page/Hong_Kong), questioning whether Gu renounced her U.S. citizenship—required for Chinese citizenship but unconfirmed by her—and suggesting financial incentives played a key role, including nearly $14 million (about 100 million yuan) in payments over three years from the Beijing Municipal Sports Bureau, a Chinese government entity, to Gu and another athlete, with $6.6 million allocated in 2025 for preparing for the 2026 Winter Olympics, separate from her overall $23 million in 2025 earnings primarily from endorsements, as revealed in a public budget document later edited to remove their names.[[3]](#ref-3)[[8]](#ref-8)[[9]](#ref-9)[[10]](#ref-10) Gu has maintained dual cultural ties, enrolled at [Stanford University](/page/Stanford_University) in California—where she primarily resides but is currently on leave for the 2026 Olympics—while endorsing Chinese state media narratives and avoiding criticism of Beijing's [human rights](/page/Human_rights) record, which some analysts attribute to pragmatic career [calculus](/page/Calculus) rather than ideological alignment.[[2]](#ref-2)[[11]](#ref-11) Beyond [skiing](/page/Skiing), she pursues modeling and business ventures, leveraging her fame for endorsements that underscore her status as a cross-cultural athletic phenomenon.[[4]](#ref-4)

## Early Life and Background

### Family Origins and Upbringing

Eileen Gu, born on September 3, 2003, in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco), [California](/page/California), holds U.S. citizenship by birth and acquired Chinese citizenship through naturalization in 2019 to compete for China, is the daughter of an American father and a Chinese mother named Yan Gu (Chinese: 谷燕).[[12]](#ref-12)[[13]](#ref-13) Yan Gu, a first-generation immigrant from mainland [China](/page/China), was born in [Shanghai](/page/Shanghai) to parents who worked as government engineers—her mother in the Ministry of Transport and her father in a related field—and emigrated to the [United States](/page/United_States) in her twenties, approximately three decades prior to Gu's Olympic debut.[[14]](#ref-14)[[15]](#ref-15) The name and professional details of Gu's father have not been publicly disclosed in reliable reports.[[16]](#ref-16)
Gu was primarily raised by her mother and maternal grandmother, Geng Guozhen, in San Francisco's affluent Sea Cliff neighborhood, where her family resided in a multimillion-dollar home overlooking the [Golden Gate Bridge](/page/Golden_Gate_Bridge).[[15]](#ref-15)[[17]](#ref-17) Her mother, who worked in [investment banking](/page/Investment_banking) after immigrating, acted as a [single parent](/page/Single_parent) and emphasized [discipline](/page/Discipline) and academic rigor, enrolling Gu in the elite Hamlin School for elementary [education](/page/Education) and later the Urban School of San Francisco.[[15]](#ref-15) Yan Gu, a former part-time ski instructor, introduced her daughter to [skiing](/page/Skiing) at age three during family outings, fostering early exposure to the sport amid a childhood that included annual summer visits to [Beijing](/page/Beijing) to connect with [extended family](/page/Extended_family).[[18]](#ref-18)[[19]](#ref-19) This bicultural environment, blending American urban life with Chinese heritage, contributed to Gu's fluency in Mandarin and her self-described identity as a "[third culture kid](/page/Third_culture_kid)."[[2]](#ref-2)

### Initial Interest in Sports and Education

Eileen Gu first took up [skiing](/page/Skiing) at age three in the [Lake Tahoe](/page/Lake_Tahoe) region of [California](/page/California), where her family traveled for the activity despite not living nearby.[[4]](#ref-4) Her mother, recognizing Gu's fearlessness, prioritized early [ski](/page/Ski) lessons to channel her energy into the sport.[[20]](#ref-20) By age eight, Gu had joined the freeski team at [Northstar California](/page/Northstar_California) Resort, marking the start of structured training in freestyle disciplines like [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) and [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle).[[4]](#ref-4)
Parallel to her athletic pursuits, Gu demonstrated strong academic interests from a young age, balancing rigorous schooling with frequent travel for competitions.[[21]](#ref-21) She attended the Katherine Delmar Burke School, an independent girls' school in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco), during which time she won nine U.S. Ski and Snowboard Association (USASA) national titles in age-division and open-class events in [Colorado](/page/Colorado) from April 2013 to April 2018.[[22]](#ref-22) To accommodate her skiing schedule, Gu accelerated her education, completing two years of high school coursework in one and graduating early.[[23]](#ref-23) Her academic prowess was evident in a near-perfect SAT score of 1580 out of 1600, reflecting a self-described "nerd" inclination toward subjects like quantum physics alongside her sports focus.[[21]](#ref-21)

## Athletic Development and Achievements

### Training and Coaching Influences

Gu began freestyle skiing at age three in the Lake Tahoe region of [California](/page/California), where her mother, Yan Gu, enrolled her in lessons and served as an instructor to foster her interest in the sport.[[24]](#ref-24)[[25]](#ref-25) By age eight, she joined the competitive ski team at [Northstar California](/page/Northstar_California) Resort in [Truckee, California](/page/Truckee,_California), benefiting from the area's advanced terrain parks and coaching resources that contributed to her technical development in [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle), and [big air](/page/Big_air) disciplines.[[4]](#ref-4)[[26]](#ref-26)
Her mother's influence extended beyond initial exposure, guiding key decisions such as specializing in [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) over alpine events and prioritizing high-risk tricks, which Yan Gu supported through rigorous oversight of training regimens and competition selections.[[27]](#ref-27) This parental involvement, combined with access to U.S.-based facilities like those in [Lake Tahoe](/page/Lake_Tahoe), provided Gu with elite-level progression unavailable in many other regions, enabling early mastery of advanced maneuvers such as the double cork 1440.[[20]](#ref-20)
In her competitive phase, Gu trained under coaches including Jamie Melton, head of China's national [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) and [big air](/page/Big_air) programs, who emphasized precision in aerial execution during her preparation for international events post-2019.[[28]](#ref-28)[[29]](#ref-29) Misra Noto Torniainen also played a pivotal role, highlighting Gu's mental preparation through detailed visualization techniques that allowed consistent performance under pressure, as evidenced in her Olympic runs.[[30]](#ref-30)[[31]](#ref-31) While her foundational skills were honed in American programs, integration with Chinese coaching after her nationality switch incorporated structured national team drills, though critics note her pre-switch U.S. training as the primary driver of her technical edge.[[20]](#ref-20)

### Key Early Competitions and Breakthroughs

Gu entered international [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) competitions during the 2017–18 season, consistently placing in the top 10 in [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) and [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) events.[[32]](#ref-32) By age 16, she had secured three podium finishes in FIS [World Cup](/page/World_cup) events, marking her emergence as a junior prospect.[[33]](#ref-33)
Her first major breakthrough came on January 27, 2019, when, at age 15, she won her maiden FIS Freeski [World Cup](/page/World_cup) title in slopestyle at [Seiser Alm](/page/Seiser_Alm), [Italy](/page/Italy), scoring 84.40 points on her third run.[[34]](#ref-34) [[35]](#ref-35) This victory highlighted her technical proficiency and competitive poise in a senior-level field.
At the 2020 Winter [Youth Olympic Games](/page/Youth_Olympic_Games) in [Lausanne](/page/Lausanne), [Switzerland](/page/Switzerland), Gu achieved a historic [trifecta](/page/Trifecta), winning gold in halfpipe on January 20, gold in [big air](/page/Big_air) on January 22 with a score of 81.50, and silver in slopestyle.[[36]](#ref-36) [[37]](#ref-37) These medals, earned while competing for the [United States](/page/United_States), established her as a dominant force in youth-level [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) across multiple disciplines.
Further solidifying her pre-Olympic credentials, Gu debuted at the [X Games](/page/X_Games) Aspen in January 2021, becoming the first woman to win three medals in her inaugural appearance: gold in [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle), gold in [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), and bronze in [big air](/page/Big_air).[[38]](#ref-38) This feat underscored her versatility and adaptability in high-stakes, invitation-only competitions.

### Post-2022 Career Trajectory and Recent Incidents

Following the [2022 Winter Olympics](/page/2022_Winter_Olympics), Gu maintained dominance in FIS [Freestyle Skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) [World Cup](/page/World_cup) events, securing multiple victories across [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle), and [big air](/page/Big_air) disciplines despite recurring injuries. In the 2023/24 season, she overcame a shoulder injury to claim four [World Cup](/page/World_cup) titles, including a [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) win at Chongli, [China](/page/China), on December 16, 2023.[[47]](#ref-47) Her performance escalated in 2024, with a [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) victory at Cardrona, [New Zealand](/page/New_Zealand), on September 9, 2024, marking her 15th career [World Cup](/page/World_cup) win and contributing to her record as the athlete with the most FIS Freeski [World Cup](/page/World_cup) victories.[[48]](#ref-48) By December 2024, Gu had tied then surpassed the all-time record with her 16th win at Secret Garden, [China](/page/China) (halfpipe, December 7), and 17th at Copper Mountain, [United States](/page/United_States) (halfpipe, December 21), scoring 90.50 on her first run to edge out competitors.[[49]](#ref-49) [[50]](#ref-50) In January 2025, she added a [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) win at Laax, [Switzerland](/page/Switzerland), on January 17—her first in that event since 2020—featuring a double 10 on the final kicker.[[51]](#ref-51)
Gu also excelled at X Games events, winning gold in women's ski superpipe at Aspen 2024 despite prior injuries, becoming the second woman to claim the title twice. At [X Games](/page/X_Games) Aspen 2025, she placed fourth in ski street style after a fall but withdrew from [big air](/page/Big_air) and [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) due to resulting injuries. In June 2025, she joined the Snow League as a global [ambassador](/page/Ambassador), aligning with her participation in its inaugural halfpipe circuit event scheduled for December 4–6, 2025, near [Beijing](/page/Beijing), [China](/page/China). Reports from September 2025 indicate she achieved two gold medals and one bronze in [big air](/page/Big_air) at the FIS Freeski World Championships, marking her as the first freeskier to win multiple golds in a single edition.[[2]](#ref-2) [[52]](#ref-52) [[53]](#ref-53)
Gu's trajectory has been punctuated by injuries, including contusions and withdrawals during the 2024/25 season that limited her starts to 12 World Cup appearances, yielding 10 wins and two second places. A notable incident occurred on August 15, 2025, during off-season training at Cardrona Alpine Resort, New Zealand, where she suffered a "very terrible accident," requiring hospitalization via stretcher and airlift; Gu hinted in a social media post on August 16 that an interruption—possibly by an overzealous fan—contributed, calling it "very dangerous." No further updates were provided by late August 2025, raising concerns about her preparation for the 2026 Winter Olympics, following a pattern of setbacks like her January 2025 X Games injuries.[[2]](#ref-2) [[54]](#ref-54) [[55]](#ref-55) Despite these challenges, Gu recovered and posted strong results in the 2025/26 FIS Freestyle Ski World Cup season prior to the Olympics, including 29th place in slopestyle at the season opener in Stubai, Austria; first place in halfpipe at Secret Garden, China, on December 13, 2025 (91.75 points, her 19th World Cup win); and first place in slopestyle at Laax, Switzerland, on January 17, 2026 (her 20th career World Cup victory).[[56]](#ref-56)[[57]](#ref-57) As of February 23, 2026, she ranked second in halfpipe FIS points, eighth in slopestyle, and low in big air (137th), with limited appearances in the latter discipline attributable to her focus on Olympic preparation.[[1]](#ref-1)
At the 2026 Milano Cortina Winter Olympics, Gu defended her halfpipe title with a gold medal performance on February 22, 2026, but shared heartbreaking news at the subsequent press conference: her grandmother, Feng Guozhen, who had been instrumental in her upbringing and teaching her Chinese culture, had passed away. Gu apologized for arriving late to the conference due to receiving this news.
Following the conclusion of the Games in late February 2026, Gu remained in Italy to participate in [Milan Fashion Week](/page/Milan_Fashion_Week) (February 24–March 2, 2026), describing modeling as her "other job" and expressing excitement about exploring creativity and femininity through fashion in contrast to her athletic career. She attended events and appeared in outfits that drew public attention.
Upon returning to the United States in early March 2026, Gu served as the grand marshal of San Francisco’s annual Chinese New Year Parade on March 7, 2026, an honor in her native city where she was celebrated as a hometown hero alongside Mayor Daniel Lurie.
Gu is expected to resume her studies at [Stanford University](/page/Stanford_University) as a junior in international relations following the Olympics, after taking leave to prepare and compete.

## Nationality Switch and Geopolitical Implications

### Background on Dual Heritage and Eligibility

Eileen Gu, born on September 3, 2003, in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco), [California](/page/California), possesses dual ethnic heritage as the daughter of an American father of European descent and a Chinese mother, Yan Gu, who was born in [Beijing](/page/Beijing) and immigrated to the [United States](/page/United_States) in her twenties to pursue studies, eventually earning an MBA from [Stanford University](/page/Stanford_University). Her mother, who worked as a ski instructor near [Lake Tahoe](/page/Lake_Tahoe) and raised Gu primarily as a [single parent](/page/Single_parent), instilled strong cultural ties to [China](/page/China), including fluency in Mandarin and annual summer visits to the country, where Gu studied in Beijing and grew to love Chinese culture. Gu has expressed pride in both her Chinese roots—cultivated through this time in Beijing and her fluent Mandarin—and her American upbringing.[[58]](#ref-58)[[12]](#ref-12)[[15]](#ref-15)[[4]](#ref-4)[[59]](#ref-59)[[60]](#ref-60)
Gu acquired U.S. citizenship automatically by birth on American soil, granting her eligibility to represent the [United States](/page/United_States) in international competitions under [International Olympic Committee](/page/International_Olympic_Committee) (IOC) rules, which require athletes to hold the nationality of the country they compete for. Her maternal lineage provided ancestral eligibility for [China](/page/China), a jus sanguinis nation, though [Chinese nationality law](/page/Chinese_nationality_law) does not automatically confer citizenship to children born abroad to a Chinese parent if the parent is deemed "settled" overseas, as Gu's mother was after immigrating and establishing residence in the U.S. prior to her birth.[[16]](#ref-16)
In 2019, at age 15, Gu obtained Chinese citizenship through naturalization, a process approved under China's Nationality Law for those with special contributions or ties, enabling her to meet IOC nationality requirements for representing China.[[61]](#ref-61) The International Ski Federation (FIS), governing body for freestyle skiing, permitted her change of national affiliation from the U.S. to China that year, as she had not yet competed at the senior international level for the U.S., complying with FIS rules allowing such switches after a two-year waiting period from last representation or under exceptions for athletes without prior senior commitments.[[16]](#ref-16)[[61]](#ref-61) The IOC Executive Board subsequently endorsed the change, confirming her eligibility for the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics under China's flag despite prior junior-level competitions for the U.S.[[61]](#ref-61) China's non-recognition of dual nationality raised questions about whether Gu formally renounced U.S. citizenship, though no public U.S. records confirm this, and she has competed exclusively for China since the switch.[[62]](#ref-62)

### Decision Process and Motivations

Gu first considered representing [China](/page/China) around age 11, shortly after [Beijing](/page/Beijing) was awarded the [2022 Winter Olympics](/page/2022_Winter_Olympics) in [2015](/page/2015), viewing it as an opportunity to promote [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) in her mother's homeland where the sport was underdeveloped.[[63]](#ref-63) By 2019, at age 15, she formalized the decision following consultations with her family and coaches, announcing her intent to compete internationally for [China](/page/China) starting that season to focus on growing [winter sports](/page/Winter_sports) participation among Chinese youth.[[64]](#ref-64)[[65]](#ref-65)
In interviews, Gu articulated her motivations as centered on cultural heritage and sport development, stating she aimed to "introduce freeskiing to girls and kids in [China](/page/China), where the sport is only just taking off" and inspire broader engagement in [skiing](/page/Skiing) amid [China](/page/China)'s push to expand its winter sports infrastructure ahead of the Olympics.[[23]](#ref-23)[[65]](#ref-65) She emphasized personal agency in the choice, describing it as a way to honor her dual background while maximizing her influence on a nascent freestyle scene, rather than competing in the more established U.S. program where she had already achieved youth-level success. Ahead of the 2026 Winter Olympics, Gu defended her decision, stating it allowed her to build the sport in a developing area rather than a saturated one like the U.S., noting, "The U.S. already has the representation. I like building my own pond."[[66]](#ref-66)[[67]](#ref-67)[[60]](#ref-60)
Gu has maintained that the decision was not driven by financial incentives, despite subsequent endorsement opportunities in [China](/page/China), but by a desire to effect change and serve as a "bridge between cultures" through athletic performance.[[64]](#ref-64) Amid vitriol and identity scrutiny, Gu highlighted double standards for mixed-race athletes, noting, “Because I’m mixed, it’s not OK. But if I was fully Chinese and I dyed my hair blond, it actually would be fine.” She has described feeling like she carries "the weight of two countries" and has grown stronger from online hate and threats, including death threats and physical assaults.[[60]](#ref-60)[[68]](#ref-68) Critics, however, have attributed pragmatic elements to the process, including [China](/page/China)'s aggressive [recruitment](/page/Recruitment) of overseas ethnic Chinese talent to bolster [Olympic medal](/page/Olympic_medal) prospects and access to state-supported [training](/page/Training) resources, evidenced by substantial payments from the Beijing Municipal Sports Bureau totaling nearly $14 million (about 100 million yuan) over three years to Gu and figure skater Zhu Yi, including $6.6 million allocated in 2025 for preparation toward the 2026 Winter Olympics, as revealed in a public budget document later edited to remove their names.[[69]](#ref-69)[[67]](#ref-67)[[70]](#ref-70) though Gu has countered such views by highlighting her commitment to grassroots inspiration over elite competition advantages. The International Ski Federation approved the nationality change in late 2019, aligning with rules allowing switches before senior international debut, which facilitated her transition without prior senior representation for the U.S.[[64]](#ref-64)

### Citizenship Status and International Sports Rules

Eileen Gu, born Anna Feng Gu on September 3, 2003, in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco), [California](/page/California), to an American father and Chinese mother, acquired [United States](/page/United_States) citizenship automatically by birth under the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.[[39]](#ref-39) [[2]](#ref-2)
On June 30, 2019, at age 15, Gu publicly announced her switch of international sporting allegiance from the [United States](/page/United_States) to [China](/page/China), citing a desire to inspire youth in her mother's homeland; this followed her affiliation change with the International Ski Federation (FIS) from U.S. Ski & Snowboard to the Chinese Ski Association.[[16]](#ref-16) [[71]](#ref-71) The FIS approved the transfer under International Competition Rules (ICR) Article 203.5, which requires proof of citizenship in the new nation, two years' residency (waivable if a parent holds that nationality), a release from the prior national association, and FIS Council approval by May 1; Gu, having competed only at junior levels for the U.S. and benefiting from her mother's Chinese nationality, met these criteria without prior senior international FIS appearances barring the switch.[[72]](#ref-72) [[61]](#ref-61)
International Olympic Committee (IOC) rules, per [Olympic Charter](/page/Olympic_Charter) Rule 41 and By-Law to Rule 41, mandate that athletes represent only their [national Olympic committee](/page/National_Olympic_Committee) (NOC) and hold its nationality, defined by citizenship or equivalent legal ties; changes require [IOC](/page/International_Olympic_Committee) Executive Board approval, a three-year cooling-off period after last representing the prior NOC (waivable or inapplicable if no prior Olympic/[World Championship](/page/World_championship) representation), and acceptance by the new NOC.[[73]](#ref-73) Gu's case qualified as she had not yet competed at senior [World Cup](/page/World_cup) or Olympic levels for the U.S., enabling her eligibility for [China](/page/China) in events like the 2022 [Beijing](/page/Beijing) Winter Olympics.[[61]](#ref-61)
China's Nationality Law (1980) prohibits dual citizenship (Article 3) and requires renunciation of foreign nationality upon naturalization (Article 8), with state media such as CGTN reporting Gu's acquisition of Chinese citizenship on June 6, 2019, implying compliance.[[71]](#ref-71) [[16]](#ref-16) However, Gu has repeatedly sidestepped direct questions on her U.S. citizenship status, stating in February 2022 press conferences that she possesses "two passports" without elaboration, while U.S. State Department policy treats individual renunciations as private and provides no public confirmation.[[74]](#ref-74) [[75]](#ref-75) No official U.S. record of renunciation exists in public databases as of 2025, though her Olympic representation of China necessitates Chinese nationality under IOC standards, fueling ongoing ambiguity and debate over whether she formally relinquished U.S. citizenship or navigates via unreported naturalization.[[76]](#ref-76) [[77]](#ref-77)
This opacity persisted post-Beijing, as Gu was named a Team USA ambassador for the [Los Angeles](/page/Los_Angeles) 2028 Olympic bid in June 2022, a role typically aligned with U.S. ties but not requiring [citizenship](/page/Citizenship) disclosure.[[78]](#ref-78) Chinese authorities, including the New York consulate, have asserted she holds [permanent residency](/page/Permanent_residency) or naturalized status sufficient for competition, but IOC eligibility hinges on effective [nationality](/page/Nationality) alignment rather than public transparency. As of 2026, Gu continues to represent China in international competitions, including the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics, but has not publicly clarified her citizenship status. China does not recognize dual citizenship, and no confirmed changes to her nationality status have been reported for 2025 or 2026, maintaining the existing ambiguity around U.S. renunciation.[[60]](#ref-60)[[79]](#ref-79)

## Controversies Surrounding Representation and Views

### Backlash in the United States

Eileen Gu's announcement in 2019 to compete for [China](/page/China), followed by her [gold medal](/page/Gold_medal) wins at the 2022 [Beijing](/page/Beijing) Winter Olympics, elicited sharp criticism in the United States, with detractors accusing her of betraying her birth country amid escalating U.S.-[China](/page/China) geopolitical tensions.[[80]](#ref-80)[[81]](#ref-81) Conservative media outlets, including [Fox News](/page/Fox_News), labeled her decision as ungrateful and a shameful "reverse migration," arguing she had reaped the benefits of American opportunities—such as training at U.S. facilities and access to elite coaching—only to abandon them for a rival nation.[[82]](#ref-82)[[83]](#ref-83)
Public figures amplified the backlash; former U.N. Ambassador [Nikki Haley](/page/Nikki_Haley) urged Gu to "pick a side," implying her choice undermined U.S. interests, while [social media](/page/Social_media) users branded her a "traitor" for prioritizing [China](/page/China) despite her American upbringing and likely eligibility for the U.S. Olympic team.[[84]](#ref-84)[[81]](#ref-81) Critics further highlighted her reluctance to address [China](/page/China)'s human rights issues, such as those in [Xinjiang](/page/Xinjiang) and [Hong Kong](/page/Hong_Kong), viewing her silence as tacit endorsement of an authoritarian regime at a time when the U.S. government had pursued diplomatic boycotts of the Olympics over such concerns.[[8]](#ref-8)[[64]](#ref-64)
Compounding the controversy was uncertainty over her citizenship status; Gu has not publicly confirmed renouncing U.S. citizenship, and her name does not appear in the U.S. State Department's quarterly lists of expatriations, raising questions about whether she retained dual benefits while adhering to international rules requiring exclusive allegiance for Olympic competition.[[16]](#ref-16)[[85]](#ref-85) Accusations of financial opportunism also surfaced, with some claiming her switch was motivated by lucrative endorsement deals in China and direct payments from government entities, such as nearly $14 million (about 100 million yuan) over three years from the Beijing Municipal Sports Bureau for training and Olympic preparation, rather than heritage alone, though Gu attributed her choice to cultural ties and competitive opportunities.[[64]](#ref-64)[[86]](#ref-86)[[9]](#ref-9) The backlash extended to online harassment, including threats, reflecting broader frustrations over perceived disloyalty in a period of heightened national security scrutiny toward China.[[81]](#ref-81) This pattern of criticism persisted into subsequent events, including at the 2026 Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics, where BBC coverage on February 15 highlighted the controversy involving Gu Ailing competing for China and Alysa Liu (Liu Meixian) for the United States, igniting social media debates on transnational identity, loyalty, and broader US-China geopolitical tensions that transcended sports.[[87]](#ref-87)

### Chinese Government Utilization and Domestic Criticisms

Following her two gold medals and one silver at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, the Chinese government and state-controlled media intensively promoted Eileen Gu as an emblem of national success and the appeal of competing under China's banner, aligning with efforts to showcase the country's capacity to integrate overseas ethnic Chinese talent into its sports system.[[69]](#ref-69) This promotion was supported by substantial financial investments from state entities; a 2025 budget document from the Beijing Municipal Sports Bureau revealed allocations of nearly 100 million yuan (approximately $14 million) over three years to Gu and another athlete for training and preparation, including about 48 million yuan ($6.6 million) in 2025 specifically for the 2026 Winter Olympics, though the document was later edited to remove their names.[[9]](#ref-9) State broadcaster [CCTV](/page/Balša_Koprivica) aired a video [interview](/page/Interview) with Gu immediately after her [big air](/page/Big_air) gold on February 8, 2022, in which she discussed eating traditional dumplings to celebrate, attracting 2.5 million viewers and amplifying her image as a relatable "daughter of the motherland."[[88]](#ref-88) This coverage extended to portraying her achievements as evidence of China's "[soft power](/page/Soft_power)" and progress in global sports dominance, with official narratives emphasizing her ethnic heritage over unresolved questions of her [citizenship](/page/Citizenship) status.[[89]](#ref-89) Such utilization served [propaganda](/page/Propaganda) goals by countering international criticisms of the Olympics hosting and highlighting naturalized athletes as beneficiaries of state investment in facilities and training.[[69]](#ref-69)
Despite widespread adulation, domestic commentators urged restraint in elevating Gu to a symbol of unwavering [patriotism](/page/Patriotism). In a February 13, 2022, [social media](/page/Social_media) post, [Hu Xijin](/page/Hu_Xijin), former editor-in-chief of the state-affiliated [Global Times](/page/Global_Times), explicitly cautioned that propaganda should confine itself to her "athletic success and Olympic performance," arguing that at age 18, Gu's desire to embody both Chinese and American identities could lead to disillusionment if she later prioritized U.S. interests or reverted allegiances.[[90]](#ref-90) Hu's intervention reflected broader elite concerns about over-idealizing figures with Western upbringings, potentially undermining nationalist cohesion if expectations of [loyalty](/page/Loyalty) proved unmet.[[89]](#ref-89)
Gu encountered direct backlash from Chinese netizens for perceived cultural and political disconnects. On February 10, 2022, her [Instagram](/page/Instagram) response suggesting users "download a VPN—it's literally free on the [App Store](/page/App_store)" to circumvent the Great Firewall and access platforms like [Instagram](/page/Instagram) was censored on [Weibo](/page/Weibo) after circulating widely, sparking accusations of [elitism](/page/Elitism) since VPNs require government approval and are effectively inaccessible or illegal for ordinary citizens without connections.[[91]](#ref-91)[[92]](#ref-92) Critics labeled her response tone-deaf to the realities of domestic internet controls, portraying her as privileged and out of touch with average Chinese experiences.[[93]](#ref-93) In May 2022, a farewell video depicting her departing [China](/page/China) via private jet drew ire for ostentation and insufficient [patriotism](/page/Patriotism), with users questioning her commitment amid her U.S.-based lifestyle.[[94]](#ref-94)
More recently, nationalist sentiments intensified scrutiny of Gu's international associations. In August 2024, videos surfaced of her dancing closely with French swimmer [Léon Marchand](/page/Léon_Marchand) at a post-Paris Olympics event, prompting accusations of being "two-faced" (liangmianpai) since Marchand had been vilified by Chinese online communities for "arrogance" after appearing to ignore a [handshake](/page/Handshake) from a Chinese competitor.[[95]](#ref-95) Gu rebutted the [criticism](/page/Criticism) on [August 22](/page/August_22), 2024, via [Instagram](/page/Instagram), citing her accumulation of 39 medals for [China](/page/China) across competitions and challenging detractors on their contributions.[[96]](#ref-96) These episodes underscore persistent domestic skepticism toward her loyalty, with some viewing her as opportunistically leveraging Chinese resources and fame while retaining Western ties, despite her athletic contributions.[[97]](#ref-97)

### Specific Political Statements and Silences

Eileen Gu has maintained that she avoids engaging in political discussions, particularly regarding geopolitical issues involving China, while publicly expressing support for certain U.S.-based movements such as Black Lives Matter, including impassioned pleas in America, emphasizing her focus on sports and [personal identity](/page/Personal_identity) rather than geopolitical issues. In interviews leading up to and during the 2022 Beijing Olympics, she stated her desire to "unite people" through her platform without delving into contentious topics, framing her nationality choice as a means to promote common understanding between the [United States](/page/United_States) and [China](/page/China).[[98]](#ref-98) She has reiterated this apolitical stance, noting in a New York Times interview that she prefers not to discuss politics related to [China](/page/China), prioritizing her athletic achievements over commentary on international affairs.[[99]](#ref-99)
Gu's public record includes few explicit political endorsements or criticisms. When pressed on human rights concerns during the Olympics, she responded that she is "not trying to solve world problems," a remark made in the context of queries about China's policies, which was later censored in Chinese media alongside her comments on navigating censorship.[[100]](#ref-100)[[92]](#ref-92) She has not issued statements condemning specific Chinese government actions, such as the suppression of pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong in 2019 or allegations of mass detentions in Xinjiang. Similarly, Gu has remained silent on the 2021 disappearance and subsequent controlled reappearance of Chinese tennis player Peng Shuai following her accusation of sexual assault against a high-ranking Communist Party official, despite international calls for athletes to address the incident.[[101]](#ref-101)
Regarding Taiwan, Gu has not publicly affirmed or rejected the "one China" principle explicitly, though her decision to represent the [People's Republic of China](/page/People) aligns with its territorial claims, as international sports bodies require competitors to adhere to national eligibility without endorsing separatist views. Critics have interpreted her silence on Taiwan's status and cross-strait tensions as implicit acceptance of Beijing's position, given China's non-recognition of dual nationality and her promotion of cultural ties to her mother's homeland. This pattern of reticence extended to halting [Western media](/page/Western_media) interviews during the Olympics amid persistent questions on these topics, a move attributed to the pressure of geopolitical scrutiny on a young athlete. No verified statements from Gu post-2022 Olympics indicate a shift toward more vocal political engagement as of October 2025.

## Commercial Success and Public Persona

### Endorsement Deals and Financial Gains

Following her successes at the [2022 Winter Olympics](/page/2022_Winter_Olympics), Eileen Gu secured endorsement deals with over 20 brands, generating substantial income primarily from the Chinese market where her visibility as a national hero amplified commercial opportunities.[[102]](#ref-102)[[103]](#ref-103) In [2021](/page/2021) alone, these partnerships yielded approximately $31.4 million in earnings, reflecting pre-Olympic momentum from her [X Games](/page/X_Games) and [World Cup](/page/World_cup) performances.[[103]](#ref-103)
Gu's sponsors span luxury fashion, sports apparel, and consumer goods, including global names like [Louis Vuitton](/page/Louis_Vuitton), [Tiffany & Co.](/page/Tiffany_&_Co.), [IWC Schaffhausen](/page/IWC_Schaffhausen), [Red Bull](/page/Red_Bull), [Victoria's Secret](/page/Victoria), Estée Lauder, Beats by Dre, and Faction Skis, alongside Chinese firms such as [Anta Sports](/page/Anta_Sports), Bosideng International Holdings, [Luckin Coffee](/page/Luckin_Coffee), [Bank of China](/page/Bank_of_China), Cadillac China, and [China Mobile](/page/China_Mobile).[[104]](#ref-104)[[105]](#ref-105)[[106]](#ref-106) By early 2022, she had expanded to at least 23 brands, adding entities like [Porsche](/page/Porsche) and others post-Games.[[107]](#ref-107) These deals leverage her appeal in both Western and Asian markets, with Chinese endorsements providing the bulk of revenue due to state media promotion and domestic consumer enthusiasm.[[108]](#ref-108)
Annual endorsement income has remained high, estimated at $22 million as of 2024 and $23 million in 2025, supplemented by modest prize winnings of around $100,000 from competitions; these commercial earnings are separate from government funding for Olympic preparation, such as $6.6 million allocated from Beijing's municipal budget to support her representation of China at the 2026 Winter Olympics.[[104]](#ref-104)[[10]](#ref-10)[[70]](#ref-70) Gu has personally reviewed her contracts since age 13, negotiating terms without intermediaries, which has supported her [financial independence](/page/Financial_independence).[[109]](#ref-109) Cumulative earnings have propelled her net worth to between $20 million and $32 million by late 2024, positioning her among the top-earning female athletes globally, though behind [tennis](/page/Tennis) stars in recent [Forbes](/page/Forbes) rankings.[[110]](#ref-110)[[111]](#ref-111)[[104]](#ref-104)

### Modeling, Media Appearances, and Business Activities

Gu signed with IMG Models, joining the agency's roster alongside supermodels such as [Bella Hadid](/page/Bella_Hadid) and [Kate Moss](/page/Kate_Moss), and has since featured in high-profile fashion campaigns for brands including [Louis Vuitton](/page/Louis_Vuitton) and [Tiffany & Co.](/page/Tiffany_&_Co.)'s 2021 "Give Me The T" collection.[[112]](#ref-112)[[107]](#ref-107) In 2019, she debuted at [Paris Fashion Week](/page/Paris_Fashion_Week), invited by a Chinese brand, marking the launch of her modeling pursuits alongside her athletic training.[[113]](#ref-113) She walked the runway for [Louis Vuitton](/page/Louis_Vuitton)'s Fall/Winter 2023/2024 collection during [Paris Fashion Week](/page/Paris_Fashion_Week) in March 2023 and attended the brand's Cruise 2022/2023 show in [California](/page/California) in May 2022, alongside celebrities including [Gemma Chan](/page/Gemma_Chan).[[114]](#ref-114) On March 3, 2026, Gu attended Le Grand Dîner du Louvre, the Louvre Museum's second annual charity fundraiser held during Paris Fashion Week, wearing an ethereal Iris van Herpen couture gown featuring winged elements inspired by the Winged Victory statue.[[115]](#ref-115) Gu has appeared on covers and editorials for publications such as [Harper's Bazaar](/page/Harper) Singapore (December 2022 issue) and Vogue Singapore, emphasizing her dual identity in sports and fashion.[[116]](#ref-116)
In media, Gu starred in Red Bull's 2022 documentary series "Everyday Eileen," which chronicled her early career balancing [skiing](/page/Skiing), modeling, and academics.[[2]](#ref-2) She has given interviews to outlets including [CNN](/page/CNN), where she discussed applying academic insights from Stanford to her [skiing](/page/Skiing) and [fashion](/page/Fashion) creativity in a January 2023 segment with [Coy Wire](/page/Coy_Wire).[[117]](#ref-117) Additional appearances include Olympics.com podcasts and videos, such as a September 2025 episode previewing the Olympic season and a 2023 interview on managing her schedule while studying quantum physics at Stanford.[[118]](#ref-118)[[119]](#ref-119) Gu also featured in CGTN Europe's exclusive interview during the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she supported Chinese athletes, and in [The New York Times](/page/The_New_York_Times) discussions on her freestyle techniques.[[120]](#ref-120)[[121]](#ref-121)
Gu's business activities remain nascent, primarily integrated with her endorsement portfolio rather than independent ventures; her mother, Yan Gu, a former venture capitalist focused on China investments, has managed aspects of her [career development](/page/Career_development) since founding a [finance](/page/Finance) firm in 1997.[[122]](#ref-122) No [public records](/page/Public_records) indicate Gu's direct involvement in launching companies or personal investments as of October 2025, with her focus split between Stanford coursework, competitions, and media commitments.[[21]](#ref-21)

## Personal Life

During her time at Stanford University, Gu faced significant personal challenges related to the controversy over her national representation. She reported being physically assaulted on campus, having her dorm room robbed, and receiving death threats, incidents she has discussed publicly in the context of the vitriol directed at her decision to compete for China.[[123]](#ref-123)[[124]](#ref-124)

### Relationships and Privacy

Eileen Gu has maintained a high degree of [privacy](/page/Privacy) regarding her romantic relationships, with no publicly confirmed partners or [dating](/page/Dating) [history](/page/History) as of 2025.[[125]](#ref-125) Reputable biographical sources indicate she is possibly single, and she has not addressed personal romantic matters in interviews, focusing instead on her athletic and professional endeavors.[[125]](#ref-125)
Speculation about potential boyfriends has circulated online, including unverified claims linking her to American Casey Traina based on social media posts from 2024 depicting shared travels, such as a trip to Death Valley.[[126]](#ref-126) Similarly, in August 2024, Chinese social media users accused her of a private relationship with French swimmer Léon Marchand, citing perceived inconsistencies with her public pro-China statements, though no evidence beyond rumors and unconfirmed sightings has substantiated these claims.[[95]](#ref-95) Such allegations appear driven by nationalistic scrutiny rather than verified facts, reflecting broader tensions around her dual cultural identity rather than documented personal ties.
Gu's approach to privacy extends to her family life, where she primarily resides in California, associated with Stanford University where she is a student on leave for the 2026 Olympics, and she temporarily relocated to Scharnitz, Austria, in 2025 for training.[[127]](#ref-127)[[128]](#ref-128) When in the United States, she lives in the San Francisco Bay Area and, as a senior majoring in international relations, attends classes or studies remotely while completing assignments during travel.[[129]](#ref-129) Her activities include exercising through running, gym sessions, spin classes, or weekend skiing and training in Tahoe; socializing with friends via informal "Gu-League" basketball, hiking, board games, outings to San Francisco spots like Asian street-food markets, parties, or sorority events; and recovery routines such as cooking nutritious meals, early sleep, and reading.[[130]](#ref-130)[[60]](#ref-60) She balances these with occasional fashion shoots or modeling work, maintaining a dynamic schedule with no fixed routine.[[130]](#ref-130) She continues to maintain a close-knit household dynamic with her mother, Yan Gu—a Chinese immigrant and [single parent](/page/Single_parent) who raised her in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco)—and her maternal grandmother, Feng Guozhen, over public disclosure.[[131]](#ref-131) Her American father, whose identity remains undisclosed in [public records](/page/Public_records), has not featured prominently in her narrative, underscoring her selective sharing of personal details to shield against media intrusion amid her high-profile career.[[15]](#ref-15) This reticence aligns with her strategy of compartmentalizing private matters, avoiding the "relationship trap" she has critiqued in broader terms as a distraction for women pursuing excellence.

Eileen Feng Gu (born September 3, 2003, in San Francisco), also known by her Chinese name Gu Ailing (谷爱凌), is an American-born freestyle skier who competes internationally for China and the most decorated female freestyle skier in Olympic history with six medals.[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2) Raised in San Francisco by a Chinese immigrant mother and an American father, Gu began skiing at age three and initially competed for the United States in junior events.[[2]](#ref-2) In October 2019, she announced her intention to represent China starting from the 2020–21 season, citing opportunities to advance women's skiing in that country, though the decision aligned with China's substantial investments in winter sports infrastructure ahead of the Beijing Olympics.[[3]](#ref-3)
Gu rose to global prominence at the [2022 Winter Olympics](/page/2022_Winter_Olympics) in [Beijing](/page/Beijing), where, at age 18, she became the youngest Olympic champion in [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) history by securing gold medals in [big air](/page/Big_air) and [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), along with a silver in [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle)—the first [athlete](/page/Athlete) to medal in all three events at a single Games.[[2]](#ref-2) Her Olympic success followed early wins, including a 2019 FIS [Freestyle Skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) World Cup [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) victory at age 15 and multiple [X Games](/page/X_Games) medals.[[4]](#ref-4) Post-Olympics, she has continued dominating, achieving 20 World Cup wins by February 2026—including a halfpipe victory at Secret Garden in December 2025 (her 19th) and a slopestyle win at Laax in January 2026 (her 20th)—along with a gold medal in women's freeski halfpipe and silver medals in big air and slopestyle at the 2026 Winter Olympics, while maintaining a high podium rate in international competitions.[[1]](#ref-1)[[5]](#ref-5)[[6]](#ref-6)[[7]](#ref-7)
The switch in national allegiance generated significant controversy, particularly in the United States, where detractors viewed it as disloyalty amid geopolitical frictions and China's policies on issues like [Xinjiang](/page/Xinjiang) and [Hong Kong](/page/Hong_Kong), questioning whether Gu renounced her U.S. citizenship—required for Chinese citizenship but unconfirmed by her—and suggesting financial incentives played a key role, including nearly $14 million (about 100 million yuan) in payments over three years from the Beijing Municipal Sports Bureau, a Chinese government entity, to Gu and another athlete, with $6.6 million allocated in 2025 for preparing for the 2026 Winter Olympics, separate from her overall $23 million in 2025 earnings primarily from endorsements, as revealed in a public budget document later edited to remove their names.[[3]](#ref-3)[[8]](#ref-8)[[9]](#ref-9)[[10]](#ref-10) Gu has maintained dual cultural ties, enrolled at [Stanford University](/page/Stanford_University) in California—where she primarily resides but is currently on leave for the 2026 Olympics—while endorsing Chinese state media narratives and avoiding criticism of Beijing's [human rights](/page/Human_rights) record, which some analysts attribute to pragmatic career [calculus](/page/Calculus) rather than ideological alignment.[[2]](#ref-2)[[11]](#ref-11) Beyond [skiing](/page/Skiing), she pursues modeling and business ventures, leveraging her fame for endorsements that underscore her status as a cross-cultural athletic phenomenon.[[4]](#ref-4)

## Early Life and Background

### Family Origins and Upbringing

Eileen Gu, born on September 3, 2003, in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco), [California](/page/California), holds U.S. citizenship by birth and acquired Chinese citizenship through naturalization in 2019 to compete for China, is the daughter of an American father and a Chinese mother named Yan Gu (Chinese: 谷燕).[[12]](#ref-12)[[13]](#ref-13) Yan Gu, a first-generation immigrant from mainland [China](/page/China), was born in [Shanghai](/page/Shanghai) to parents who worked as government engineers—her mother in the Ministry of Transport and her father in a related field—and emigrated to the [United States](/page/United_States) in her twenties, approximately three decades prior to Gu's Olympic debut.[[14]](#ref-14)[[15]](#ref-15) The name and professional details of Gu's father have not been publicly disclosed in reliable reports.[[16]](#ref-16)
Gu was primarily raised by her mother and maternal grandmother, Geng Guozhen, in San Francisco's affluent Sea Cliff neighborhood, where her family resided in a multimillion-dollar home overlooking the [Golden Gate Bridge](/page/Golden_Gate_Bridge).[[15]](#ref-15)[[17]](#ref-17) Her mother, who worked in [investment banking](/page/Investment_banking) after immigrating, acted as a [single parent](/page/Single_parent) and emphasized [discipline](/page/Discipline) and academic rigor, enrolling Gu in the elite Hamlin School for elementary [education](/page/Education) and later the Urban School of San Francisco.[[15]](#ref-15) Yan Gu, a former part-time ski instructor, introduced her daughter to [skiing](/page/Skiing) at age three during family outings, fostering early exposure to the sport amid a childhood that included annual summer visits to [Beijing](/page/Beijing) to connect with [extended family](/page/Extended_family).[[18]](#ref-18)[[19]](#ref-19) This bicultural environment, blending American urban life with Chinese heritage, contributed to Gu's fluency in Mandarin and her self-described identity as a "[third culture kid](/page/Third_culture_kid)."[[2]](#ref-2)

### Initial Interest in Sports and Education

Eileen Gu first took up [skiing](/page/Skiing) at age three in the [Lake Tahoe](/page/Lake_Tahoe) region of [California](/page/California), where her family traveled for the activity despite not living nearby.[[4]](#ref-4) Her mother, recognizing Gu's fearlessness, prioritized early [ski](/page/Ski) lessons to channel her energy into the sport.[[20]](#ref-20) By age eight, Gu had joined the freeski team at [Northstar California](/page/Northstar_California) Resort, marking the start of structured training in freestyle disciplines like [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) and [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle).[[4]](#ref-4)
Parallel to her athletic pursuits, Gu demonstrated strong academic interests from a young age, balancing rigorous schooling with frequent travel for competitions.[[21]](#ref-21) She attended the Katherine Delmar Burke School, an independent girls' school in [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco), during which time she won nine U.S. Ski and Snowboard Association (USASA) national titles in age-division and open-class events in [Colorado](/page/Colorado) from April 2013 to April 2018.[[22]](#ref-22) To accommodate her skiing schedule, Gu accelerated her education, completing two years of high school coursework in one and graduating early.[[23]](#ref-23) Her academic prowess was evident in a near-perfect SAT score of 1580 out of 1600, reflecting a self-described "nerd" inclination toward subjects like quantum physics alongside her sports focus.[[21]](#ref-21)

## Athletic Development and Achievements

### Training and Coaching Influences

Gu began freestyle skiing at age three in the Lake Tahoe region of [California](/page/California), where her mother, Yan Gu, enrolled her in lessons and served as an instructor to foster her interest in the sport.[[24]](#ref-24)[[25]](#ref-25) By age eight, she joined the competitive ski team at [Northstar California](/page/Northstar_California) Resort in [Truckee, California](/page/Truckee,_California), benefiting from the area's advanced terrain parks and coaching resources that contributed to her technical development in [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle), and [big air](/page/Big_air) disciplines.[[4]](#ref-4)[[26]](#ref-26)
Her mother's influence extended beyond initial exposure, guiding key decisions such as specializing in [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) over alpine events and prioritizing high-risk tricks, which Yan Gu supported through rigorous oversight of training regimens and competition selections.[[27]](#ref-27) This parental involvement, combined with access to U.S.-based facilities like those in [Lake Tahoe](/page/Lake_Tahoe), provided Gu with elite-level progression unavailable in many other regions, enabling early mastery of advanced maneuvers such as the double cork 1440.[[20]](#ref-20)
In her competitive phase, Gu trained under coaches including Jamie Melton, head of China's national [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) and [big air](/page/Big_air) programs, who emphasized precision in aerial execution during her preparation for international events post-2019.[[28]](#ref-28)[[29]](#ref-29) Misra Noto Torniainen also played a pivotal role, highlighting Gu's mental preparation through detailed visualization techniques that allowed consistent performance under pressure, as evidenced in her Olympic runs.[[30]](#ref-30)[[31]](#ref-31) While her foundational skills were honed in American programs, integration with Chinese coaching after her nationality switch incorporated structured national team drills, though critics note her pre-switch U.S. training as the primary driver of her technical edge.[[20]](#ref-20)

### Key Early Competitions and Breakthroughs

Gu entered international [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) competitions during the 2017–18 season, consistently placing in the top 10 in [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle) and [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) events.[[32]](#ref-32) By age 16, she had secured three podium finishes in FIS [World Cup](/page/World_cup) events, marking her emergence as a junior prospect.[[33]](#ref-33)
Her first major breakthrough came on January 27, 2019, when, at age 15, she won her maiden FIS Freeski [World Cup](/page/World_cup) title in slopestyle at [Seiser Alm](/page/Seiser_Alm), [Italy](/page/Italy), scoring 84.40 points on her third run.[[34]](#ref-34) [[35]](#ref-35) This victory highlighted her technical proficiency and competitive poise in a senior-level field.
At the 2020 Winter [Youth Olympic Games](/page/Youth_Olympic_Games) in [Lausanne](/page/Lausanne), [Switzerland](/page/Switzerland), Gu achieved a historic [trifecta](/page/Trifecta), winning gold in halfpipe on January 20, gold in [big air](/page/Big_air) on January 22 with a score of 81.50, and silver in slopestyle.[[36]](#ref-36) [[37]](#ref-37) These medals, earned while competing for the [United States](/page/United_States), established her as a dominant force in youth-level [freestyle skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) across multiple disciplines.
Further solidifying her pre-Olympic credentials, Gu debuted at the [X Games](/page/X_Games) Aspen in January 2021, becoming the first woman to win three medals in her inaugural appearance: gold in [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle), gold in [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), and bronze in [big air](/page/Big_air).[[38]](#ref-38) This feat underscored her versatility and adaptability in high-stakes, invitation-only competitions.

### Olympic and [World Championship](/page/World_championship) Performances

At the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing, Eileen Gu competed for China and secured three medals across the women's freeski events, becoming the first freestyle skier to achieve this feat in a single Games.[[39]](#ref-39) In the big air event on February 8, she won gold with a final-run score of 94.50 for a left double cork 1620, achieving a total of 188.25 points.[[40]](#ref-40) Gu earned silver in slopestyle on February 15 after a fall on her final run prevented a potential gold.[[41]](#ref-41) She claimed her second gold in halfpipe on February 18.[[42]](#ref-42)

Following the [2022 Winter Olympics](/page/2022_Winter_Olympics), Gu maintained dominance in FIS [Freestyle Skiing](/page/Freestyle_skiing) [World Cup](/page/World_cup) events, securing multiple victories across [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe), [slopestyle](/page/Slopestyle), and [big air](/page/Big_air) disciplines despite recurring injuries. Gu also excelled at X Games events, winning gold in women's ski superpipe at Aspen 2024 despite prior injuries, becoming the second woman to claim the title twice. At [X Games](/page/X_Games) Aspen 2025, she placed fourth in ski street style after a fall but withdrew from [big air](/page/Big_air) and [halfpipe](/page/Half-pipe) due to resulting injuries. In June 2025, she joined the Snow League as a global [ambassador](/page/Ambassador), aligning with her participation in its inaugural halfpipe circuit event scheduled for December 4–6, 2025, near [Beijing](/page/Beijing), [China](/page/China).
